subject: chemistry
title: Buffer solutions
key_idea: A buffer solution keeps its pH almost constant when small amounts of acid or alkali are added, or when it is diluted. An acidic buffer holds a weak acid and its conjugate base, and the pH is found from Ka and the ratio of the two.

sections.heading: What a buffer is and how to make one

blocks.text: A buffer needs a reservoir of both a weak acid and its conjugate base. This section covers the definition and two ways to make one.

items.meaning: A solution that minimises changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
A weak acid and its conjugate base, usually supplied as a salt.
A weak base and its conjugate acid, usually supplied as a salt.

items: It also keeps its pH approximately constant when diluted.
It works only for small additions. A large amount of acid or alkali uses up one component and the pH then changes.

rows: Weak acid + a salt of that acid
Unreacted CH₃COOH and the CH₃COO⁻ formed
Weak base + a salt of that base

items: With excess weak acid and alkali, the alkali reacts with some of the acid to make its salt. What is left over is the weak acid.
The pH is set by the ratio [acid] : [conjugate base], and this is chosen by the amounts mixed.
A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base together.
It can be made from the acid and its salt, or from excess weak acid and alkali.

blocks.text: The two components are the weak acid and its conjugate base. Each removes one of the possible additions.

blocks.label: Acid buffer equilibrium
where: CH₃COOH = weak acid, present in large amount
CH₃COO⁻ = conjugate base, from the salt

items: **Acid added:** extra H⁺ reacts with the conjugate base. CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH. The equilibrium shifts left, and [H⁺] hardly changes.
**Alkali added:** OH⁻ reacts with H⁺ to make water. The weak acid then dissociates to replace the H⁺ removed. The equilibrium shifts right, and [H⁺] hardly changes.
The ratio [CH₃COOH] : [CH₃COO⁻] changes only slightly, so the pH changes only slightly.

diagram.alt: A sequencing activity. Put the steps of buffer action when acid is added into order.
diagram.prompt: Put the steps in order when a little acid is added to an ethanoic acid buffer.
steps: H⁺ reacts with CH₃COO⁻ to make CH₃COOH
The equilibrium CH₃COOH ⇌ H⁺ + CH₃COO⁻ shifts left
[H⁺] returns to almost its original value
The pH changes only very slightly

items: A **basic buffer** such as NH₃ / NH₄⁺ works in the same way: NH₄⁺ gives up H⁺ when alkali is added, and NH₃ takes up H⁺ when acid is added.
The pair NH₃ / NH₄⁺ is a weak base with its conjugate acid.
The conjugate base removes added H⁺. The weak acid replaces H⁺ removed by alkali.
The ratio of acid to base barely changes, so the pH barely changes.

sections.heading: Calculating the pH of an acidic buffer

blocks.text: The pH comes from Ka and the ratio of weak acid to conjugate base. The approximations are the same as for weak acids.

blocks.label: Hydrogen ion concentration of a buffer

items.text: Find [HA] and [A⁻] in the mixture. Use moles divided by the total volume.

blocks.text: A buffer with 0.100 mol/dm³ CH₃COOH and 0.200 mol/dm³ CH₃COO⁻ (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵): [H⁺] = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.500 = 8.7 × 10⁻⁶ mol/dm³, pH = 5.06.

items: The [A⁻] is taken as the concentration of the salt, because the acid is only slightly dissociated.
To make a buffer of a chosen pH, find [H⁺] = 10^(−pH), then the ratio [A⁻] ÷ [HA] = Ka ÷ [H⁺].
When [HA] = [A⁻], [H⁺] = Ka and pH = pKa.
pH = pKa when the acid and its conjugate base have equal concentrations.

sections.heading: Buffers in the body and in everyday life

blocks.text: Buffers hold the pH steady where a change would do harm.

items: Blood plasma is kept at pH 7.35 to 7.45 by the carbonic acid-hydrogencarbonate buffer, H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻.
Excess H⁺ reacts with HCO₃⁻ to form H₂CO₃, which breaks down to CO₂ and water. The CO₂ is breathed out.
Excess OH⁻ reacts with H⁺, and H₂CO₃ dissociates to replace the H⁺.
Buffers are also used in foods, shampoos and medicines, to keep the pH constant.
Blood is kept near pH 7.4 by H₂CO₃ / HCO₃⁻.
Buffers are used wherever pH must stay constant.

checks.q: Explain how a mixture of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate resists a change in pH when a small amount of hydrochloric acid is added.
checks.a: Ethanoate ions react with the added H⁺ to form ethanoic acid: CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺ → CH₃COOH. The equilibrium shifts left, so [H⁺] and pH hardly change.

checks.q: Calculate the pH of a buffer containing 0.200 mol/dm³ CH₃COOH and 0.100 mol/dm³ CH₃COONa (Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵ mol/dm³).
State how a buffer is made from a weak acid and a strong alkali, and why the alkali must not be in excess.
checks.a: Add alkali to an excess of the weak acid. Some acid forms its salt and the rest stays as acid. If the alkali were in excess, no weak acid would remain to give a buffer.

blocks.text: The role of the conjugate pair in pH control must be explained, and the pH of a buffer must be calculated from Ka and the equilibrium concentrations of the conjugate pair.

items: The blood buffer keeps plasma between pH 7.35 and 7.45.
In the blood buffer, H₂CO₃ is the weak acid and HCO₃⁻ is its conjugate base.

blocks.text: Preparing a buffer of a given pH

items.text: Choose concentrations or volumes of acid and salt in this ratio.

blocks.text: For pH 4.46 with Ka = 1.74 × 10⁻⁵, [H⁺] = 3.5 × 10⁻⁵, so [A⁻] ÷ [HA] = 0.50. Use twice as much acid as salt.

items: Acidic buffers contain a weak acid and the salt of that weak acid.
Basic buffers contain a weak base and the salt of that weak base.
Calculation is required for acidic buffers; the action of basic buffers is explained qualitatively.
Explanations of buffer action must use chemical equations.
Uses of buffers include the role of HCO₃⁻ in controlling the pH of blood.
